canonical.title: In-memory tokens vs cookie-backed BFF sessions under XSS: what each architecture actually buys you

parent.title: Pure React 19 SPA or a .NET 10 BFF? A decision framework for an internal admin console

siblings.title: Does the IETF browser-based-apps BCP apply to an internal admin console?
siblings.summary: The BCP names "business applications" in its strongest recommendation, so an internal console is in scope — but the ranking is a security/simplicity trade-off, not a normative MUST.

siblings.title: Refresh tokens and silent renew in a browser SPA (2026)
siblings.summary: Iframe silent renew is dead cross-site but alive same-site; refresh-token rotation works on both stacks, DPoP only really works on Keycloak, and TanStack Query needs a single-flight mutex either way.

siblings.title: Greenfield BFF vs retrofitting later: where the asymmetry actually is
siblings.summary: Adding a BFF later is a two-way door — if you build the SPA with one auth module, one fetch wrapper, relative paths and no client-side JWT parsing. The one-way door is the API, not the frontend.

siblings.title: What a BFF costs you every day: OpenAPI codegen and the local dev loop
siblings.summary: A path-preserving BFF leaves OpenAPI codegen essentially untouched — the real daily cost is one extra process, a Vite proxy config, and losing Swagger UI 'Try it out'.

siblings.title: BFF options in .NET 10: Duende.BFF, YARP, or hand-rolled
siblings.summary: If you build a BFF, the realistic .NET 10 choice is YARP + AddOpenIdConnect + the free Apache-2.0 Duende.AccessTokenManagement (~250 LOC you own), or Duende.BFF if you qualify for its free Community Edition; Duende.BFF's paid entry point is $5,750/yr.

sources.title: IETF — OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications (draft-26)
sources.claim: IETF draft maps XSS attack scenarios per architecture: BFF blocks token theft and new-token acquisition but leaves 'Proxying Requests via the User's Browser' open; browser-based OAuth client is vulnerable to all scenarios.

sources.title: Pragmatic Web Security (Philippe De Ryck) — Localstorage & XSS
sources.claim: Philippe De Ryck argues avoiding localStorage is the wrong fix: XSS gives full control over application code, so in-memory/worker-hidden tokens are also reachable.

sources.title: FusionAuth — Backend for Frontend security architecture
sources.claim: FusionAuth: BFF's only remaining XSS vector is request proxying/session riding; the Sept 2025 npm supply-chain compromise showed malicious JS can steal anything JS can read.

sources.title: OWASP — HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: OWASP: do not store session identifiers in local storage; a single XSS can steal everything in Web Storage; prefer sessionStorage over localStorage when persistence is not needed.

sources.title: Microsoft MSRC — Weaponizing XSS: when one bug isn't enough (Nov 2025)
sources.claim: Microsoft MSRC (Nov 2025): XSS is a gateway risk; injected script triggers state-changing requests in the authenticated session; defenses must be layered.

sources.title: Schellman — Demonstrating impact with cross-site scripting
sources.claim: Pentester walkthrough: with HttpOnly set, XSS still performs authenticated actions via XHR from the user's browser context and reads responses to lift anti-CSRF tokens.

sources.title: web.dev — Mitigate XSS with a strict Content Security Policy
sources.claim: web.dev: nonce/hash-based strict CSP with strict-dynamic blocks untrusted inline scripts and javascript: URIs, but does not stop injections into a nonced script body, dynamically created script locations, AngularJS template injection, or eval sinks.

sources.title: Google Research / ACM CCS 2016 — CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!
sources.claim: Google/ACM CCS 2016 internet-scale study: 94.68% of script-limiting CSP policies were ineffective; allowlist-based CSP is largely bypassable, motivating nonce + strict-dynamic.

sources.title: URIports — CSP and Trusted Types
sources.claim: Trusted Types enforces safe DOM manipulation at the sink level; Safari 26 (Sept 2025) and Firefox (Feb 2026) shipped it, reaching Baseline; a no-op policy still provides false security.

sources.title: MDN — CSP: require-trusted-types-for
sources.claim: MDN: require-trusted-types-for disallows raw strings at DOM XSS injection sinks, requiring values produced by a Trusted Types policy.

sources.title: Duende — BFF Security Framework documentation
sources.claim: Duende BFF: browser never sees tokens, server-side session state, server can forcibly end sessions, built-in CSRF protection via a required custom header; session hijacking is acknowledged as hard to fully prevent.

sources.title: Auth0 — Things developers get wrong about the BFF pattern
sources.claim: Auth0: BFF shifts the security boundary rather than eliminating it; tokens in memory are as reachable as tokens in localStorage; the trade is XSS token theft for a more constrained CSRF surface.

sources.title: Hacker News — Keycloak / Angular / BFF thread
sources.claim: HN thread on Keycloak/Angular/BFF: contrarian commenter horsawlarway argues httpOnly cookies only add marginal complexity for an attacker who can script the page directly; TobbenTM defends BFF as keeping session tokens server-side.

sources.title: Tore Nestenius — The BFF pattern explained (ASP.NET Core)
sources.claim: HttpOnly cookies are still automatically attached to same-origin fetch/XHR issued by JavaScript — the mechanical basis of session riding.

sources.title: Duende — How BFF helps secure single-page applications
sources.claim: Duende's marketing framing: with BFF, an XSS-compromised browser app carries no risk of access-token theft.

sources.title: Hacker News — token storage thread (unscaled)
sources.claim: HN commenter unscaled: HttpOnly cookies are genuinely better security-wise; storing refresh tokens in local storage is only for low-security use cases.

sources.title: Chrome for Developers — Trusted Types (Lighthouse best practices)
sources.claim: Chrome docs: Trusted Types blocks risky injection points such as .innerHTML from accepting unvalidated string values.
